articles.title: On Liberalism’s Global Career: Dadabhai Naoroji and Representative Government
articles.abstract: This article reconsiders the relationship between the globalization of political liberalism and the globalization of political equality. Departing from interpretations of liberal theories of rights and representation as egalitarian or democratic, the article reconstructs an elitist paradigm of liberal representative government from the colonial world. It does so by offering a new reading of the thought of Indian political leader Dadabhai Naoroji. It recovers Naoroji’s overlooked commentary on political representation and imperial reform. I show that Naoroji drew upon analyses made by the first generation of Indian liberal thinkers about imperial political economy and mass-elite relations and used these arguments to formulate a distinctive model of electoral politics as a form of hierarchical tutelage. The recovery of Naoroji’s theory illustrates the deep tensions between representation and mass politics that marked liberalism’s global circulation.

articles.title: The Ambiguities of Ownership and Class: A Reply to Nicholas Vrousalis
articles.abstract: The article replies to Nicholas Vrousalis’s attempt to rescue radical republicanism from my critique that it fails on three counts: its non-contingency, domination, and structural injustice theses. Central to my response are the claims that (i) capitalist power cannot be reduced to legal ownership of the means of production, as the process of capitalization is constitutive of capital; (ii) neither neo-republican nor Kantian notions of domination adequately capture what is inherently wrong with capitalism, and (iii) the concept of “class domination” remains theoretically puzzling. I then defend an alienation-centered critique: capitalism’s mode of investment subjects citizens to an impersonal and anarchical form of governance, which, by being necessarily alienating, contradicts democratic self-determination. Overall, this critique forms the core of a “political, political theory of capitalism” and grounds the case for a specific kind of democratic socialism—socialism as reconciliation—which is more demanding than both republican and liberal socialisms.

articles.title: The Symbolic Politics of Housing
articles.authors: DAVID E. BROOCKMAN, CHRISTOPHER S. ELMENDORF, JOSHUA L. KALLA
articles.abstract: Voter opposition to development contributes to America’s housing shortage. Prevailing explanations emphasize NIMBYism (opposition to housing nearby) and homeowners’ self-interest. However, homeownership often fails to predict housing policy views, while NIMBYism offers little insight into support for policies that do not concern specific proposed housing projects—the focus of much recent policymaking. Drawing on symbolic politics theory, we argue that voters’ affect toward groups that housing policies make salient powerfully shapes their judgments about housing policies. We present evidence supporting this theory. Experiments show that affect toward developers and investors who build housing, government actors who approve it, and residents who move into it explain anti-development preferences when policies make these groups salient. Providing further causal evidence, short-form videos that manipulate affect toward developers have meaningful downstream effects on support for new development and permitting reforms. Ironically, voter dislike of the very actors who could ameliorate the housing shortage further exacerbates it.

articles.title: Perpetrator Identity and Post-Conflict Ethnic Attitudes: The Legacies of Intragroup and Intergroup Violence
articles.abstract: Researchers have extensively examined how political violence shapes social and political behavior, yet most studies focus on interethnic violence and assume a binary conflict structure. This study challenges that assumption by examining how perpetrator identity, ingroup versus outgroup, shapes postwar intergroup relations. Using original survey data from Tamil civilians in Northern Sri Lanka, we analyze exposure to intragroup and intergroup violence during Sri Lanka’s 26-year civil war, which involved substantial violence both across and within ethnic groups. We find that exposure to intragroup violence is associated with lower trust toward coethnics, reduced ingroup favoritism in attitudes and behavior, and weaker reliance on ethnic cues in political choice. In contrast, exposure to intergroup violence increases interethnic prejudice and social distance, heightens discrimination in behavioral interactions, and strengthens ethnically motivated political behavior. These findings indicate that perpetrator identity shapes the social legacies of wartime violence and can generate opposing postwar dynamics.

articles.title: Queenpins: Women Leaders and Violence in Organized Crime
articles.abstract: How does women’s leadership affect the behavior of criminal organizations? Organized criminal groups are male-dominated patriarchal organizations that use violence to govern, compete, and control territory. Qualitative research suggests that women leaders—though rare—reduce their organization’s violent behavior. We examine this expectation through Mexico’s Tijuana Cartel, leveraging the sudden 2008 ascension of a woman to leadership. Although violence increased under her tenure, synthetic control results show greater reliance on hidden violence and less on visible violence and territorial expansion. Original data on male cartel leaders reveals that systematic gender differences in trajectories help explain these patterns. Our results indicate that women leaders are not necessarily less violent than men but instead strategically employ different violent repertoires. Case studies of 44 women leaders across 18 countries since 1850 assess the broader applicability of these findings and identify important scope conditions. Our findings underscore the importance of incorporating gender into organized crime research.

articles.title: The Immigration Surplus Revisited
articles.abstract: We extend the immigration surplus results of Borjas (1995). In a closed competitive constant-returns economy, we show that an influx of migrants (holding their skill mix fixed) must increase the total real income of natives, for any number of factor inputs, any pattern of substitutability or complementarity between them, and any number of intermediate or final goods – with larger gains if natives and migrants differ more in skill mix. If natives supply labour elastically across skill types, their welfare gains are diminished, even if they respond by moving to higher-paying jobs. We illustrate our results using a US calibration.

articles.title: Networks of Dissent: Social Leaders and Protest in an Autocracy
articles.authors: Johannes Buggle, Max Deter, Martin Lange
articles.abstract: This paper examines how network ties between local social leaders influenced the diffusion of mass protests in an autocracy. We focus on the Protestant Church and the Peaceful Revolution in East Germany. To quantify the role of leader networks in protest diffusion, we compile biographical records of over 1,600 Protestant pastors and construct network ties based on shared employment histories. Our findings reveal that network connections led to an increase in protest diffusion by 7.1 percentage points in a given week. Evidence from quasi-random connections, placebo networks, and an IV strategy supports a causal interpretation of these results.

articles.title: Cognitive ability, risk preferences and errors
articles.abstract: In this paper we examine the link between cognitive ability, risk preferences and the errors that people make. We build a unique dataset that contains almost 260,000 decisions made under risk in a variety of tasks by approximately 13,000 individuals, with each person having completed a test designed explicitly to measure their cognitive ability. Our analysis suggests that intelligence has (1) no impact on risk preferences and (2) a robust link to errors. Our results have implications for the development of theories that seek to explain the impact of cognitive ability on decision making.

articles.title: Professional Networks and the Labour Market Assimilation of Immigrants
articles.authors: Olof Åslund, Mattias Engdahl, Sébastien Willis
articles.abstract: We examine how professional networks shape immigrants’ job search and labour market assimilation. Analysing displaced workers in Sweden, we show that connections to firms through conationals are especially important for immigrants’ job finding. As networks expand to include more natives, the value of such connections rises towards that seen for displaced natives. Origin homophily also predicts whether a connection provides a referral—increasing earnings and lowering turnover—rather than vacancy information. Networks account for 20 per cent of the growth in immigrants’ re-employment over their first decade after arrival; immigrants’ networks are as productive as natives’ after fifteen years.

articles.title: Income Support for Migrant Agricultural Workers: Differential Inclusion via Racialized Administrative Burdens Under Canada's Employment Insurance Program
articles.abstract: Under Canada's Seasonal Agricultural Worker Program and Agricultural Stream, migrant agricultural workers (MAWs) arriving principally from Caribbean and Latin American countries are granted entry to Canada as essential workers. Yet they have limited access to social and statutory benefits and entitlements vis‐à‐vis citizens and permanent residents. Through an inquiry into rules governing access to benefits under Employment Insurance (EI) – a national contributions‐based unemployment insurance program providing income replacement in instances of job loss, sickness, maternity, parental, and caregiving responsibilities—this article analyzes administrative mechanisms contributing to MAWs' differential inclusion. Examining EI policy administration, an underexplored area of scholarly inquiry, it demonstrates how, given the structure of migrant work programs in agriculture, seemingly neutral rules governing the provision of income replacement contribute to disentitlement among MAWs otherwise fulfilling qualifying requirements. Bridging scholarship illustrating how policy design can shape differential access to EI benefits among social groups and research documenting racialized (im)migration policies opening exclusively temporary migration to MAWs historically and contemporaneously, the analysis highlights the role of racialized administrative burdens in impeding MAWs from accessing EI's full range of income supports.

articles.title: Make It Easier, Not More Complex: Employee Views on Immigration Detention Decision‐Making in Canada
articles.authors: Bronwen Perley‐Robertson, Ralph C. Serin, Isabella R. L. Bossom, Sarah K. Watts, Shelley L. Brown
articles.abstract: Rising public scrutiny has put immigration detention systems under pressure to defend their decision‐making practices. The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) has drawn attention in this area, largely due to its partnerships with correctional agencies. Critics challenge CBSA's framework for placing noncitizens in these facilities, characterizing its risk assessment practices as opaque, arbitrary, and subjective. To address these concerns, CBSA commissioned us to develop an empirical tool for guiding immigration detention decisions—spanning conditional release to security classification level within detention. We surveyed 92 CBSA employees using mixed methods to gain their insights and ensure the operational utility of our tool. Top‐rated risk factors for decision‐making were criminal/compliance history, mental health, cooperation, identity concerns, and behaviour. We also identified misconceptions about standardized risk tools, the need for a streamlined assessment process, gaps in mental health guidance, operational decision‐making barriers, and opportunities for enhanced training. This study provides a foundation for developing an operationally useful tool that will improve the transparency and defensibility of CBSA's immigration detention decisions.

articles.title: Social Capital, Platform Power, and the Private Authority of Big Tech Firms: Theorizing The Micro-Foundations of Platform Power Among Social Networking Sites
articles.abstract: In the era of digital globalization, Big Tech firms have emerged as pivotal non-state actors in International Relations (IR). A growing body of research theorizes the political influence of these firms through the concept of platform power, which emphasizes the unique combination of economic scale and intimate relationships with their users. Despite the analytical power of the concept, past work on the platform power of Big Tech firms obscures important differences among these firms. To improve our understanding of the foundations of Big Tech’s platform power, I focus specifically on Social Networking Sites (SNSs). SNSs are platforms that provide web-based services to enable individuals to create profiles, connect with others, and share information, opinions, and media. I argue that the micro-foundation of SNSs’ platform power is their exceptional capacity to foster social capital accumulation among their users. In turn, this cultivates loyal consumer bases and ultimately enables SNSs to wield significant private authority in global politics. I demonstrate the implications of this argument for how SNSs gain, maintain, and potentially lose private authority. This conceptual framework enhances our comprehension of Big Tech’s authority and helps further investigation into the normative implications, identity dynamics, and security concerns within this evolving landscape.

articles.title: Positioning enjoyment and appreciation as key components of news use
articles.authors: Jennifer Hoewe, Brett Sherrick, Diane Jackson, Sam Woodland
articles.abstract: In response to the continued convergence and hybridization of news and entertainment media content, this research explores the roles of enjoyment and appreciation in contemporary news use. Three studies (two surveys and one experiment) show a clear link between enjoyment, appreciation, and news use. Both enjoyment and appreciation are positively related to agreement, value alignment, attitude change, and attitude reinforcement in the context of news use. News enjoyment is related to increased positive and decreased negative emotions, while news appreciation is connected to an increase in and tolerance of mixed emotions. Importantly, news enjoyment decreases actual knowledge while facilitating greater affective polarization. News appreciation increases more positive feelings toward other people. These results illustrate the value of merging research on entertainment and news media, and they also suggest that news enjoyment is a driving factor in the growth of less democratic news use outcomes.

articles.title: Academic freedom: defending a public good
articles.abstract: This essay, an expanded version of a Presidential Address delivered at the 2026 conference of the International Communication Association (ICA), addresses the global erosion of academic freedom and its implications for communication scholarship. Drawing on a survey of 546 ICA members, the article documents substantial restrictions on academic freedom, alongside widespread occupational intimidation. Most survey respondents have personally experienced hostility or intimidation related to their work, most commonly through social media and personal insults. Nearly half of them report altering their academic practice—e.g., by adjusting their teaching content and research topics or speaking out less publicly. While most attacks originate from the public and political actors, the survey shows that a significant amount of intimidation originates from colleagues and other academics. The essay argues that these findings demand a coordinated collective response, including institutional advocacy, solidarity networks, and recognition of academic freedom as an indispensable human right.

articles.title: Introducing the Peace Observatory: Peace Negotiations and Mediation in Armed Conflicts
articles.authors: Allard Duursma, Janek Bruker, Carina Diener, Samantha Gamez, Valentin Felix Geier, Arianna Guidolin
articles.abstract: This article introduces the Peace Observatory, a new global dataset that captures over 10,000 rounds of peace negotiations in interstate, intrastate, and non-state conflicts between 1989 and 2023 with regular updates planned for additional years. The Peace Observatory disaggregates peacemaking into distinct negotiation rounds. To demonstrate the value of the dataset, the article examines how the involvement of autocratic states as mediators is associated with negotiation outcomes across different phases of the peace process. Unlike many existing datasets that operate at the conflict-year level and do not systematically distinguish between stages of peacemaking, the Peace Observatory records the specific phase of each negotiation round – prenegotiation, negotiation, or implementation. This enables analysis of whether mediator characteristics matter differently at distinct stages of the process. The analysis shows that autocratic involvement is positively associated with the conclusion of peace agreements during the negotiation phase, but not in the prenegotiation or implementation phase.

articles.title: Strike when they aren’t looking: great power crises and threats to rule
articles.authors: David B Carter, İpek Ece Şener
articles.abstract: Although regime threats such as civil conflict and coup d’état are widely studied, their links to global crises receive little attention. We argue that episodes of instability among great powers ripple through the international system, encouraging violent threats to rule in less powerful states. We assess our arguments with both new and existing indicators of systemic instability and show that periods of economic and security instability among great powers are associated with a heightened risk of both civil conflict onset and regime change coup attempts in smaller states. We further demonstrate important heterogeneity in the risk faced by smaller states by showing that security instability which inflicts a given regime's great power allies drives this statistical association. Our work offers a novel explanation for the emergence of threats to rule, integrating the literatures on great power politics, civil conflict, and coup d’état, while also demonstrating why regime threats not only cluster geographically but also cluster in time. This study has important implications for contemporary international politics and for future conflict research given the widely observed increase in great power competition and systemic instability over the past decade or so.

articles.title: The demobilizing effect of violent actions and radical-right involvement on public support for protest
articles.authors: Daniel Saldivia Gonzatti, Eylem Kanol, Sophia Hunger, Swen Hutter
articles.abstract: How does radicality affect public support for protest? Despite a long-standing scholarly debate about the demobilizing power of radicality, empirical evidence beyond the use of violent action and left-libertarian social movements remains scarce. Therefore, this article advances the debate by examining the effects of two forms of radicality, violent forms of protest and radical protest actors, in the context of a right-authoritarian movement. We employ a novel and comprehensive multistep research design to study these theoretical expectations, integrating original survey and natural experimental evidence. Empirically, we draw on the case of the anti-containment protests in Germany during the COVID-19 pandemic, emblematic of the rise of right-authoritarian social movements in contemporary democracies. We examine the role of demonstrator-instigated violence and radical-right involvement in demobilizing sympathizers and likely participants. The empirical findings show that, in contrast to left-libertarian movements, individuals strongly committed to the cause are likely to continue to take to the streets regardless of the presence of violence and radical-right actors. The findings suggest adverse diminishing demobilization effects of radicality in contemporary democracies, which are less pronounced for individuals close to right-authoritarian movements.

AI can persuade people to take political actions
articles.authors: Kobi Hackenburg, Luke Hewitt, Caroline Wagner, Christopher Summerfield, Ben M. Tappin
articles.abstract: There is substantial concern about the ability of advanced AI to influence people’s behavior. A rapidly growing body of research has found that AI can produce large persuasive effects on people’s attitudes, but whether AI can persuade people to take consequential real-world actions has remained unclear. In two large preregistered experiments ( N = 17 , 950 responses from 14,779 people), we used conversational AI models to persuade participants on a range of attitudinal and behavioral outcomes, including signing real petitions and donating money to charity. We found sizable AI persuasion effects on these behavioral outcomes (e.g. + 19.7 percentage points on petition signing). However, we observed no evidence of a correlation between AI persuasion effects on attitudes and effects on behavior. Moreover, we replicated prior findings that information provision drove effects on attitudes, but found no such evidence for our behavioral outcomes. In a test of eight behavioral persuasion strategies, the strategy focused on information provision produced the smallest behavioral effect, though differences among the eight were small. Taken together, these results suggest that previous findings relying on attitudinal outcomes may generalize poorly to behavior, and therefore risk substantially mischaracterizing the real-world behavioral impact of AI persuasion.

articles.title: Calibration, accuracy, and domain variation across one million collective forecasts from prediction platforms
articles.authors: Justin Dickerson, Hilla Shinitzky, Maayan Peer, Mattan S. Ben-Shachar, Michael Gilead
articles.abstract: Using approximately one million resolved contracts and questions across four collective forecasting platforms, twelve domains, and time horizons ranging from hours to years, we evaluate the calibration and accuracy of collective forecasts in real-world settings. We found that forecast probabilities were overall highly calibrated: events assigned a probability of p % occurred approximately p % of the time. This broad pattern was evident across platforms and many domains, although fine-grained analyses revealed systematic tendencies toward over- or underestimation in highly consequential areas. While this does not mean that forecasting platforms provide certainty about individual events, our findings suggest that large-scale aggregation of judgments contains meaningful information about real-world uncertainty; when examined in aggregate, the predictions generated by the platforms provided informative estimates of event likelihood.

articles.title: Geography of groundwater use and depletion in internationally shared aquifers
articles.authors: Marc F. Müller, Kyle F. Davis, Julie Faure, Davide Danilo Chiarelli, Fengwei Hung
articles.abstract: Transboundary aquifers (TBAs) underlie 35% of global groundwater-irrigated cropland, yet few are covered by formal cooperative arrangements. Whether this limited cooperation is consequential depends in part on where groundwater is used within shared aquifers, because pumping far from international borders may generate little cross-border impact. Combining ∼ 116,000 well observations with global irrigation data across all 426 known TBAs, we assess how groundwater use and depletion differ from comparable domestic systems and how they are distributed relative to international borders. While we find no evidence of greater average depletion in TBAs, depletion is more strongly concentrated toward international borders in shared aquifers and varies substantially across systems. Irrigation is also more intensive and concentrated toward borders in shared aquifers, although much of this pattern is attenuated after accounting for border rivers. Groundwater-supplied irrigation remains more border-proximate after accounting for these rivers. A dyad-level typology distinguishes shared systems according to where groundwater demand is concentrated, linking their potential for cross-border interaction to different management options. These findings suggest that transboundary groundwater governance should be organized around the geography of groundwater use and potential cross-border interactions rather than treating shared aquifers as uniform governance units.

articles.title: Scientists disrupt less but more persistently with career aging
articles.authors: Nan Deng, Liying Yang, Shlomo Havlin, An Zeng
articles.abstract: Disruption describes the extent to which a scientific work overturns the prior knowledge on which it builds and leads to a new line of research. A scientist’s tendency to produce disruptive work has been found recently to decline over the career. However, the disruption index captures only how strongly a paper overturns prior work and ignores whether that disruption is later accepted or overturned by subsequent research. The persistent disruption (PD) framework adds this second perspective, identifying work that disrupts prior research and is then consolidated rather than displaced by later work. We examine how PD evolves over the career and find the opposite pattern: The probability of producing a persistent disruptive paper increases with career age. Senior scientists disrupt prior work less often compared to young, but once they do, the disruption tends to persist rather than being quickly superseded. Our results suggest that this reversal feature is due to the experience and we corroborate it across several dimensions of recognition. We also show that, at a fixed level of disruptiveness, the more senior the scientist is, it attracts more citations, social-media attention, and research grants. Nobel laureates also show delayed persistent disruptions. They exhibit high disruptive ability early in their careers, yet their prize-winning work appears years later. This lag further indicates that experience is needed to turn disruptive ability into the field’s most celebrated contributions.

articles.title: Linguistic intervention unlocks the economic gains of diversity
articles.authors: Sheen S. Levine, Simon Siegenthaler, Bart J. Wilson
articles.abstract: Gains from trade generate prosperity, yet interpersonal exchange can falter along racial lines. We study incentivized experimental economies where participants must spontaneously initiate and sustain trading relationships with others whose race is visible. When the highest gains from trade require cross-race exchange, diverse economies underperform: welfare and specialization suffer as many retreat to autarky. This underperformance reflects not segregation into racial trading blocs, but a collapse in exchange. Opportunities for contact alone do not close the performance gap, which persists and even widens over time. To understand why, we turn to communication itself. Lower welfare is associated with less communication, fewer expressions of affiliation and achievement, and less explicit signaling of needs, deficits, and surpluses. We call this communicative misalignment: differences in shared-language use that raise search, bargaining, and coordination costs. A brief linguistic intervention equips participants with a communicative toolkit. It increases communication volume and the frequency of motivational and state-signaling language. Crucially, when gains depend on cross-race exchange, the intervention restores specialization and cross-race trade, closing the performance gap. Its effects are minimal when efficient trade need not cross race, indicating specificity rather than generic skill training. Language thus operates bidirectionally, both revealing the state of cooperation and causally shaping it. Although we examine racial boundaries, the mechanism may operate along other fault lines where interactional norms diverge, including hierarchy, geography, or culture. Language, a primary conduit of culture, can impede exchange when misaligned and facilitate it when aligned. This suggests a scalable micro-governance tool for reducing transaction costs.

articles.title: Stringent policies were associated with greater Covid-19 vaccine uptake including among those who did not trust the vaccine
articles.authors: Manu M. Savani, Richard Koenig, Brendan Nyhan, Sanchayan Banerjee, Andrew Hunter, Peter John, Blake Lee-Whiting, Peter John Loewen, John McAndrews
articles.abstract: Are stringent vaccine promotion policies associated with higher vaccine uptake? We argue policy stringency, which changes the costs and benefits of immunisation choices, can affect individual vaccination decisions. In a survey of G-7 countries, 22% of respondents ( n = 42,417) said they did not trust the Covid-19 vaccine, but half of them reported having at least one vaccination. We investigate factors associated with take-up. Our data indicate a high-stringency policy environment (with vaccine mandates and travel restrictions) is associated with increased uptake of the initial vaccination protocol (7 percentage points) compared to a low-stringency policy environment. Among those who did not trust the Covid-19 vaccine, a high-stringency policy environment is associated with increased uptake of the initial vaccine (16 percentage points) and the booster vaccine (20 percentage points). Our findings suggest high-stringency policies can promote vaccine uptake but raise questions about how to strike the right balance between persuasive and coercive policies.

articles.title: Institutional Amnesia and the Loss of “The Why Rationale” in Central Government Agencies
articles.authors: Alastair Stark, Hridesh Gajurel, Jack Corbett, Dennis C. Grube, Heather Lovell, Rodney J. Scott
articles.abstract: Data from 115 interviews conducted with officials in the Westminster systems of Australia, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom is used to substantiate a corrosive relationship between institutional amnesia and the ability of public servants to make sense of their organizational context. A process in which public servants question why the policies, procedures, and organizational frameworks that surround them is proposed as one medium through which this relationship operates. Four problematic effects produced by this relationship and process are subsequently analyzed: (1) public servants following but not understanding procedures, (2) inexplicable organizational aspects getting abandoned, (3) the layering of new organizational features on top of old ones, creating complexity, and (4) public service inefficiencies and associated public servant frustration. The article concludes with the implications of this important relationship for public administration scholars and practitioners.

articles.title: Public Administration and the Crisis of American Democracy
articles.abstract: The field of public administration stands amid genuine crisis. Americans don't trust government or its administrators. Elected officials have attacked the career service as agents of the “deep state” and, though it might be hard to admit, many of public administration's critics have a point. Government's performance too often falls short of what people expect, practitioners too often seem too unresponsive to elected officials, and researchers too often seem to have only fuzzy guidance for practitioners. However, public administration undoubtedly is more important now than ever in translating public goals into effective action, and in bringing to life the democratic aspirations Madison and his colleagues wished for the country at its founding. The field urgently needs new strategies and tactics for solving the new generation of puzzles the country faces. In coming together, practitioners and researchers build on these puzzles to chart an exciting road forward.

articles.title: How the Public Makes Sense of Gender Politics: Textual, Emotional, and Symbolic Dimensions
articles.authors: Marta Fraile, Nerea Gándara-Guerra, Paula Zuluaga-Borrero
articles.abstract: How do ordinary citizens make sense of gender politics? While research has examined public support for feminism and gender equality either separately or as interchangeable concepts, far less is known about the meanings citizens attach to these labels and whether they evoke distinct political meanings. This article compares the textual, emotional, and symbolic associations of three related but distinct framings of gender politics: feminism, gender equality, and equality between men and women. Drawing on an original pre-registered survey experiment in Spain, respondents were randomly assigned to define and evaluate one of the three labels, allowing us to analyze their meanings across textual, emotional, and visual dimensions. We find that while most respondents express sympathy toward all three labels, feminism stands as the most contested. Feminism also has the sharpest sociopolitical profile, eliciting greater support from young, highly educated, progressive women. Text analyses reveal that the public frames feminism in terms of collective action, conflict, and women’s identity, drawing heavily on political language, while the other two labels emphasize policy and material concerns. Emotionally, gender politics elicits more positive than negative responses across all three labels, though men report slightly higher negative emotions toward feminism. Feminism is also the only label consistently associated with images of women’s mobilization and protest, reinforcing its distinctively political resonance. These findings show that feminism and gender equality tap related but meaningfully distinct constructs in the public mind, with implications for how scholars measure attitudes toward gender politics and interpret public support for equality-related policies.

articles.title: Attitudes Toward LGB and TGD Rights in Latin America
articles.authors: Oscar Castorena, Eli G Rau, Valerie Schweizer-Robinson, Elizabeth J Zechmeister
articles.abstract: Research on attitudes toward transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) individuals lags behind research on opinion on the lesbian, gay, and bisexual (LGB) population, leaving open questions about public opinion on these two LGBTQ+ subgroups, in general and in particular in the Global South. While a sizeable gap exists in US public opinion toward TGD and LGB rights, we do not know whether that finding is generalizable to other contexts. With a focus on Latin America, we draw on a range of scholarship to identify factors that could result in a similar divergence of attitudes toward these subgroups or, instead, relative convergence. Our analyses focus primarily on novel survey data from representative surveys across thirteen Latin American countries. Our results demonstrate a fair amount of convergence in mean levels, item nonresponse rates, and predictors of views on LGB versus TGD rights. We present some notable differences across countries and issues, with results for the former (countries) varying by socio-political context and the latter (issues) varying across political and nonpolitical domains. We identify these patterns as constituting a future agenda for researchers of opinion on LGBTQ+ topics. We conclude that, in the contemporary period, the Latin American public holds fairly similar mental schemas toward LGB and TGD groups.

articles.title: How New Products Enter Markets: Social Networks, Consumer Imports, and Retailer Learning
articles.authors: David Argente, Esteban Méndez, Diana Van Patten
articles.abstract: This paper studies how new varieties enter markets and become locally available. We provide causal evidence of demand externalities that operate in two steps. First, information about new varieties diffuses directly through real-world social ties among consumers. Second, early purchases generate an indirect spillover to firms: local retailers learn from “pioneer” consumers which new varieties are most likely to succeed and adjust their product offerings accordingly. We study this process in the context of direct-to-consumer imports. Using customs records on individuals’ purchases matched to population-wide social networks, international migrant links, and retailer catchment areas, we document economically meaningful demand externalities. Product-specific expenditure shocks abroad transmit through migrant networks and shift which varieties consumers purchase. Leveraging these shocks as a plausibly exogenous source of local demand variation, we show strong peer effects: prior purchases by close neighbors, coworkers, or friends increase an individual’s likelihood of purchasing the same variety, especially for premium and visible goods. We leverage this result to identify an indirect spillover from consumers to firms: retailers are more likely to add a variety to their assortment when it becomes popular among consumers in their catchment area. Combining the instrument with linked consumer–retailer data and a self-conducted retailer survey, we show that this response reflects learning about latent demand for varieties not yet stocked locally. Together, social diffusion and retailer learning generate demand multipliers that reshape local product availability and expand access to global variety.

articles.title: Optimal Flood Insurance in a Second-Best World: Fiscal Spillovers, Reclassification Risk, and Moral Hazard
articles.abstract: Intensifying climate change makes protection against natural disaster risk – either through ex ante insurance or ex post aid – a first-order public policy issue. Flood risk protection in the U.S. traditionally featured ex post aid through FEMA and heavily subsidized insurance through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). In an effort to correct subsidy-induced overbuilding and under-mitigation in flood-prone areas, the NFIP recently moved to actuarially fair insurance premiums. But this change has two unintended consequences: a fiscal spillover onto FEMA disaster aid as insurance coverage declines in flood-prone areas, and household exposure to uninsurable reclassification risk from uncertain climate projections. We develop a model of optimal flood insurance that incorporates the static and dynamic tradeoffs of subsidizing premiums. We then use a variety of identification strategies and data to estimate the five key parameters needed to implement this model. We find that the fiscal spillover and reclassification risk protection benefits significantly outweigh the moral hazard costs, and that the optimal subsidy to flood insurance is 51%, comparable to the level of subsidization before the recent reform.

articles.title: When Should We (Not) Interpret Linear IV Estimands as LATE?
articles.abstract: In this paper I revisit the interpretation of the linear instrumental variables (IV) estimand as a weighted average of conditional local average treatment effects (LATEs). I focus on a situation in which additional covariates are required for identification while the reduced-form and first-stage regressions may be misspecified due to an implicit homogeneity restriction on the effects of the instrument. I show that the weights on some conditional LATEs are negative and the IV estimand is no longer interpretable as a causal effect under a weaker version of monotonicity, i.e. when there are compliers but no defiers at some covariate values and defiers but no compliers elsewhere. The problem of negative weights disappears in the interacted specification of Angrist and Imbens (I1995), which avoids misspecification and seems to be underused in applied work. I illustrate my findings in an application to the causal effects of pretrial detention on case outcomes. In this setting, I reject the stronger version of monotonicity, demonstrate that the interacted instruments are sufficiently strong for consistent estimation using the jackknife methodology, and present several estimates that are economically and statistically different, depending on whether the interacted instruments are used.

articles.title: Robust Aggregation of Correlated Information
articles.authors: Henrique de Oliveira, Yuhta Ishii, Xiao Lin
articles.abstract: Decisions are typically made by drawing on multiple sources of information, yet the correlation among these sources is often hard to assess. We study robustly optimal strategies—those that maximize the worst-case payoff guarantee across all correlation structures. With two states and two actions, the robustly optimal strategy is strikingly simple: use only the best information source and ignore the rest. With more actions, a robustly optimal strategy decomposes the problem into local comparisons and assigns each comparison to the source that is best at that comparison. With more states, the same specialization logic survives through a concavification characterization: the decision problem is decomposed into payoff-relevant components, and each component is assigned to its best source. These results offer a new rationale for why ignoring information can be optimal and highlight the benefit of using specialized information sources when correlations are ambiguous.

articles.title: Parental Response to Fetal Shocks and Macroeconomic Volatility
articles.abstract: We examine parental response to a fetal shock using data from 150 Demographic and Health Surveys in 50 developing countries. Focusing on the impact of Ramadan fasting, a common shock experienced by more than a billion Muslims worldwide, we find that children exposed to Ramadan fasting during pregnancy have lower rates of full vaccination for DPT and polio compared to their non-exposed siblings. Further, parents tend to compensate for the fetal shock during booms and reinforce during economic downturns. Our estimations suggest that this has resulted in approximately half a million excess infant deaths over the past three decades.

articles.title: The Female Sensitivity Hypothesis: Evidence From Experimental Economics
articles.authors: Felipe A. Araujo, Neeraja Gupta, Lise Vesterlund
articles.abstract: We assess the empirical evidence for the hypothesis that women more than men respond to changes in treatment. First, we examine whether the results of over two hundred experimental economics papers support the female sensitivity hypothesis. Second, using data from two studies (DellaVigna and Pope, 2022; Exley et al., 2025), we conduct over two hundred pairwise tests of the hypothesis. Both analyses show that gender is not predictive of responsiveness to treatment. We further examine how the hypothesis has been disseminated in the literature and find that it is referenced predominantly by papers that support it.

articles.title: The Equilibrium Effect of Information in Consumer Credit Markets: Public Records and Credit Redistribution
articles.abstract: Information is central to consumer credit, but little is known about its equilibrium effects. We study a 2017 natural experiment in which non-bankruptcy public records were purged from U.S. credit reports. The large information-removal differences across states allow us to identify equilibrium impacts. Available credit increased for consumers who lost negative information directly. Consistent with our model, available credit declined indirectly for consumers who did not lose the negative information because they could no longer distinguish themselves. The direct and indirect effects nearly canceled, so the net equilibrium effect after a year was nearly zero but with substantial redistribution.

articles.title: Hostility, Population Sorting, and Backwardness: Quasi-Experimental Evidence from the Red Army after WWII
articles.abstract: How can short episodes of localized hostility shape regional economic trajectories that even amplify over time? I exploit economic differences across the idiosyncratic and short-lived line of contact between the Red Army and the Western Allies in South Austria at the end of WWII. The 74-day hostile presence of the Red Army shaped the age- and occupation-structure via refugee flows, causing amplifying demographic effects over time and backwardness in sector development and tax revenues. My findings also point to the isolated role of the Red Army’s hostile actions after WWII in understanding the European economic East-West divide.

articles.title: Structuring Cash Transfers: Cash Flow Preferences, Seasonality, and Financial Decisions in Rural Kenya
articles.authors: Carolina Kansikas, Anandi Mani, Paul Niehaus
articles.abstract: We examine the preferences of low-income households in Kenya over the structure of unconditional cash transfers. Most preferred lumpy transfers, and some preferred deferred receipt—in contrast to the typical structures of safety-net programs, but consistent with evidence on the financial challenges of poverty. Turning to consequences, receiving transfers later in the year raised income 1.5 years later—but willingness to defer receipt was sensitive to small changes in cash flow around the time of decision-making. Taken together, these results illustrate how adapting cash transfer design to the decision-making environment of those in poverty could improve financial choices and outcomes.

articles.title: Blended Finance and Female Entrepreneurship
articles.authors: Halil İbrahim Aydın, Çağatay Bircan, Ralph De Haas
articles.abstract: We study the real and allocative consequences of relaxing gender-specific credit constraints by analyzing a blended finance program designed to expand bank lending to female entrepreneurs in Turkey. Merging credit registry, tax, and matched employer-employee data, we find participating banks raised their credit share to women by over 18%, spanning repeat, poached, and first-time borrowers. Beneficiary firms invest more, grow employment, sales, and profits, diversify their networks, and exit less. Treated banks also expand lending to male entrepreneurs, though the increase is smaller and disproportionately directed toward higher-productivity firms, suggesting reallocation rather than crowding out. District-level effects are absent, reecting the program’s modest scale.

articles.title: How Credible Are the Findings from Online Experiments?
articles.authors: Abel Brodeur, Nikolai Cook, Anthony Heyes, Lamis Kattan
articles.abstract: Online experiments have surged in popularity, but how credible are their published results? We examine the universe of hypotheses tested on Amazon Mechanical Turk and reported in leading journals between 2010 and 2021. We find evidence of widespread p-hacking, publication bias, and under-powered studies. The extent of the problems varies substantially across fields, with marketing particularly badly afflicted and little evidence of distortion in economics. We explore correlates of increased credibility and compare the online results to laboratory results from the same outlets, finding similar distortions in both, with bunching just above the significance threshold more pronounced on MTurk.

articles.title: Tax Incentives and Return Migration
articles.abstract: We study how tax incentives affect the return migration of high-skilled expatriates to their home country, exploiting a generous income tax break for returnees in Italy. Using administrative data and a Triple-Difference design, we estimate a migration elasticity to the average net-of-tax rate just below one. Responses are sizable across the upper half of the earnings distribution, indicating that tax-induced migration is not limited to top earners. A cost-benefit analysis reveals that, while costly in the short term, the scheme pays for itself in present value if a sufficiently large fraction of returnees remains after the scheme elapses.

articles.title: Contracting Structures in Public Procurement: Evidence from Donor-Funded Electrification in Kenya
articles.authors: Catherine D. Wolfram, Edward Miguel, Eric Hsu, Susanna B. Berkouwer
articles.abstract: We study how contracting and monitoring structures in public procurement affect large-scale infrastructure construction. Starting in 2016, Kenya’s public electric utility ran competitive auctions and then awarded and administered dozens of procurement contracts to connect millions to electricity. The causal analyses leverage natural and experimental variation and granular, independentlycollected construction quality data. Kenya Power contracts funded by the World Bank featured unbundled contract components known as ‘design-bid-build’ and enhanced monitoring compared to African Development Bank-funded contracts. Unbundling contracts delayed construction progress but improved quality. Randomized inspections improved quality without large delays. Bundled contracting with additional independent monitoring could improve outcomes.

articles.title: Is American Soft Power a Casualty of the Trade War? Evidence from U.S. Movie Viewership in China
articles.authors: Haichao Fan, Yichuan Hu, Lixin Tang, Shang-Jin Wei
articles.abstract: The US trade war against China can either enhance or diminish American soft power in China, depending on whether Chinese citizens view it as legitimate. We study how US movie viewership, a measure of American soft power, responds to the trade war. We find a significantly greater reduction in US movie viewership in regions more exposed to the Trump tariffs, but no corresponding decline in non-US movies. The decline is stronger for action and drama movies, which tend to embody greater perceived “Americanness.” Survey data also show a sharper decline in trust in Americans in more tariff-exposed regions.

articles.title: How Competition Shapes Peer Effects: Evidence from a University in China
articles.abstract: Competition is widely used to enhance effort and performance. However, in many domains, like education, competition could backfire, as performance is not solely reliant on individual efforts but also on collaboration endeavors among peers. Utilizing university administrative data, we examine how competition changes peer effects and peer interactions. Exploiting randomly assigned roommates, we first demonstrate that high-ability roommates have detrimental effects on the academic performance of high-ability students. More importantly, such negative peer effects significantly increase along various dimensions of competition intensity within dorm rooms. Follow-up survey findings reveal that competition hinders mutual assistance and fosters unfriendly behaviors among roommates.

articles.title: Estimating Substitution Patterns and Demand Curvature in Discrete-Choice Models of Product Differentiation
articles.authors: Cameron Birchall, Debashrita Mohapatra, Frank Verboven
articles.abstract: We extend BLP’s aggregate discrete-choice model of product differentiation to create more flexibility in the price functional form. We apply a Box-Cox specification, which relaxes the typical unit demand assumption and creates flexibility on demand curvature. The model provides a unifying framework for mixed logit and mixed CES models, while remaining computationally tractable. We provide an illustrative application to the ready-to-eat cereals market. This shows that the cross-sectional relation between price elasticities and average prices per product is more in line with descriptive elasticity patterns, and that substitution between product pairs may be affected to some extent.

articles.title: Democracy Doesn’t Always Happen Over Night: Regime Change in Stages and Economic Growth
articles.abstract: How substantial are the economic benefits from democratic regime change? We argue that democratization is often not a discrete event but a two-stage process: autocracies enter into “episodes” of political liberalization, which eventually culminate in regime change or not. To account for this chronology and the implicit counterfactual groups, we introduce a repeated-treatment difference-in-difference implementation capturing nonparallel trends and selection into treatment. We find that modeling regime change in two stages rather than a single event yields stronger long-run growth effects. Among democratizers, experiencing repeated episodes without regime change reduces growth in democracy, whereas length of episode does not.

articles.title: Structuralizing the stress process: states as contextual determinants of stress and mental health
articles.authors: Rachel Donnelly, Zhe Zhang, Mateo P Farina, Blake W Powell
articles.abstract: Despite growing evidence that policy environments influence mental health, we have limited knowledge of how policy environments influence the stress processes that shape mental health. This study develops and tests a theoretical framework that structuralizes the stress process model by explicating how the state policy context (1) directly influences mental health, (2) indirectly influences mental health via stress exposure, and (3) mitigates the impact of stressors on mental health. This study uses nationally representative data from the Household Pulse Survey (2020–2023; n = 3,043,961) and the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS; 2015–2019; n = 1,989,932) merged with state policy liberalism data to consider how state policy liberalism—the ideological orientation of state policies—shapes mental health. Results show that more liberal state policies were associated with lower odds of probable depression, probable anxiety, and frequent mental distress and weakened associations between three focal economic stressors—income loss, financial hardship, employment status—and mental health outcomes. Moreover, the association between state policy liberalism and mental health was partially mediated by financial hardship. Findings differed slightly by age: mediation via financial hardship was more evident among older adults (65+), whereas the buffering of economic-related stressors was mostly among adults under sixty-five. Overall, this study demonstrates the importance of a structuralized stress process model for mental health research.

articles.title: Leaving together: social influence and church decline
articles.abstract: Church membership has declined across much of the Western world in recent decades. Existing research has identified individual characteristics that affect individuals’ likelihood of leaving their churches, but far less is known about how social interactions influence church decline. We examine (1) how exposure to others leaving the Church of Sweden affects individuals’ likelihood of leaving and (2) the aggregate membership dynamics generated by these micro-level processes. Using full-population register data from 2002 to 2023 and a dynamic matched-sample design, we estimate social-influence effects and assess how susceptibility varies with religious embeddedness, defined as the extent to which individuals are socially connected to other church members. We use these estimates to calibrate an agent-based simulation model linking individual behavior to aggregate membership decline. The results show that exposure to leavers increases individuals’ likelihood of leaving the Church, particularly among those with weak religious embeddedness. The simulations indicate that social influence contributed appreciably to the numerical decline of the Church of Sweden, while religious embeddedness moderated this effect. Social influence can thus amplify ongoing religious decline, while religious embeddedness attenuates this amplification.

articles.title: Review of “Family Legal Vulnerability: How Immigration Policy Shapes the Lives of Latino College Students”
Nonstandard work, nonstandard lives? Temporary employment, unemployment, and family transitions
articles.abstract: It is well documented that unemployment is closely associated with family outcomes, affecting the occurrence, timing, and sequencing of key family transitions. Individuals with unemployment experience are more likely to postpone marriage, enter cohabiting unions, transition into parenthood outside marriage, and experience partnership dissolution. Temporary employment is often regarded as a better alternative because it provides income, opportunities for skill accumulation, and continued attachment to the labor market. In reality, however, temporary jobs are characterized by substantial insecurity and strain, which may have important consequences for family lives. Applying discrete-time event history analysis to nationally representative longitudinal data from the British household panel study, I show that temporary employment constitutes a meaningful source of uncertainty with substantial consequences for family formation and stability. The consequences of employment insecurity vary by educational attainment, gender, and union type. Educational differences strongly condition men’s family responses to employment insecurity, while for women education primarily structures exposure rather than buffering its consequences. Cohabitation functions as an adaptive response to unemployment but not to temporary employment, which is instead associated with greater instability of cohabiting unions. Together, these findings highlight the importance not only of employment, but of stable employment, for family formation and stability.

articles.title: Framing Democracy: How Elites' Discourse Shapes Citizens' Understandings of Democracy and Enables Backsliding
articles.abstract: abstract: Citizens' divergent understandings of democracy have important implications for democratic resilience, yet the sources of this heterogeneity remain contested. The author argues that partisan elite discourse is a key driver of these divergent understandings: political leaders' framing of democracy systematically shapes their supporters' democratic priorities. Observational and experimental evidence from Turkey supports this argument. The author establishes that Turkish party leaders differ in how they conceptualize democracy in public discourse, and these differences map onto their supporters' understandings of democracy. A population-based survey experiment shows that when leaders emphasize particular dimensions of democracy, copartisans also assign greater importance to those same dimensions of democratic governance. These findings highlight how partisan elite framing can influence mass conceptions of democracy in ways that enable democratic backsliding: would-be autocrats can exploit this dynamic to subvert liberal norms without significant backlash, even where overall support for democracy remains high.

articles.title: The Paradox of Imperial Taxation: How Diversity Shaped Fiscal Development in the Ottoman Empire
articles.abstract: abstract: This article investigates the relationship between diversity and state building by examining how diversity affects the costs of investing in fiscal capacity. The author argues that diversity—ethnic or religious—makes populations less legible to the state, thereby increasing those costs. Higher costs deter the state from investing in fiscal capacity in more diverse areas, which hinders fiscal capacity building in those regions. Instead, the state diverts investments to less diverse areas, which are typically populated by the core/dominant group. As a result, the dominant group bears a higher tax burden compared to minority groups, which do not experience comparable tax increases. The author tests these arguments using original data on local-level fiscal revenues in the late Ottoman Empire along with qualitative and quantitative evidence from archival sources and contemporary cross-national and subnational data.

articles.title: Political Socialization In Authoritarian Regimes: Sites and Everyday Experiences for Young People in Zimbabwe
articles.authors: Marjoke Oosterom, Simbarashe Gukurume, Tinotenda Chishiri
articles.abstract: abstract: Scholarship on political socialization has largely overlooked how forms of violence and repression experienced by young people living in authoritarian regimes affect their political development. Bringing together the literatures on political socialization and violence, this study aims to advance debates on youth political socialization in authoritarian regimes. How and where do young people in such contexts develop political orientations and behaviors, and through which mechanisms? To address these questions, this study draws on qualitative research with urban youths in Zimbabwe between 2019 and 2022 to demonstrate the significance of everyday encounters with authoritarianism in contested urban spaces. The authors advance existing scholarship by conceptualizing and analyzing diffuse socialization experiences and sites of socialization, showing how ruling party agents operating at urban markets use diverse socialization practices to cultivate loyalty to the ruling party among young traders. The authors argue that political socialization in this context does not foster genuine loyalty but provides tacit knowledge about authoritarian politics and how to navigate it through performative compliance.

articles.title: Renewing Democracy: How Exposure to Electoral Turnovers Reinforces Citizens' Democratic Support
articles.abstract: abstract: A prevailing narrative argues that citizens who live under democratic rule take it for granted, potentially leading to democratic backsliding. This article advances a more optimistic perspective, arguing that electoral turnovers—that is, elections that displace the head of government—reinforce democratic support. To test this argument, the author merges multiple international surveys that cover more than 350,000 respondents in seventy-nine countries, matches those surveys with a century's worth of electoral data, and identifies the national electoral turnovers to which each respondent was exposed throughout their life. Cohort analysis shows that exposure to turnovers, especially those that occur after prolonged periods of incumbency, has a positive and lasting effect on democratic support. Further analysis reveals that the effect is positive in a wide range of contexts, but is strongest among citizens who have always lived in a democracy. This finding thus suggests that frequent electoral turnovers are important to renew citizens' support for democracy.

articles.title: When Does Civil Society Prevent Violence? Civic Networks, Demography, and Communal Conflict in Côte d'Ivoire
articles.abstract: abstract: This article explores whether local civic networks can reduce the risk of violence in communally divided societies. The author argues that dense associational networks can foster intercommunal peace near elections, but only when those networks are situated in communities diverse enough that civic networks foster intergroup contact and monitoring by local elites. Leveraging new village-level data and interviews from Côte d'Ivoire, the author examines the relationship between the country's civic associations and the political violence that occurred during national elections in 2020 and 2021. Contrary to the arguments of civil society skeptics, he shows that robust networks of voluntary associations had significant spillover benefits for peace, particularly in communally diverse areas. However, in areas with a dominant communal group, civic networks had little impact on the risk of violence. The findings inform debates about the constraints on intercommunal conflict and the significance of associationalism in divided societies.

articles.title: Structure and agency in emancipatory reform: A blueprint from a Black union
articles.abstract: The National Labor Convention of 1869, the first of its kind for African American workers, yielded a grand strategy for achieving full emancipation, in which those long subjected to domination might attain durable independence. Drawing upon decades of Black republican thought, this agenda combined macro‐level reforms targeting agrarian and industrial monopolies with micro‐level interventions into the habits of the working class. While the project fell short, its multivalent approach nevertheless offers republican theorists today a framework for better understanding the structural dynamics of domination and how to overcome them.

articles.title: Two Paths of Conversation: How Stories and Statistics are Associated With Community Engagement in Online Debate Surrounding Vaccine Science Skeptical Content
articles.authors: Han Li, Inhwan Bae, Pengfei Zhao, Natalie Bazarova, Drew Margolin
articles.abstract: Statistical and narrative evidence represent two distinct ways of substantiating claims in public reasoning, but does this distinction matter for how people engage with vaccine science skeptical (VSS) content and the discursive spaces surrounding it? This study addresses this question through a large-scale, LLM-assisted observational analysis of online engagement with VSS posts and comments that support or counter such content using statistical versus narrative evidence in the Reddit community r/DebateVaccines . Building on Fisher’s distinction between rational and narrative paradigms , we theorize two paths of conversation through which evidentiary forms are associated with audience engagement with contentious vaccine discourses in a naturalistic social media setting: a rational pathway, marked by concentrated participation and corrective contestation around statistical claims and counterclaims, tending toward a single evidence-based truth “approved” by one-click reactions; and a narrative pathway, characterized by generative engagement featuring broader and more distributed participation, more discursive and generative engagement, and greater acceptance of competing viewpoints. These findings provide a springboard for theorizing evidentiary form as a key epistemic logic associated with how conversations evolve in real-world engagement with contentious, socially consequential issues such as vaccine misinformation, while informing hybrid approaches to addressing skepticism toward established vaccine science.

articles.title: Constantly Connected, Differently Affected: Response Speed Shapes Parents’ and Adolescents’ Feelings of Connection
articles.authors: Razieh Pourafshari, Miriam Brinberg, Joseph B. Bayer
articles.abstract: Response speed in digital communication serves as a signal of availability, yet past research has overlooked how speed expectations in specific relationships translate into social connection. This study addresses this oversight by integrating theoretical perspectives on constant connectivity and chronemics to test the implications of perceived response speed for parent-adolescent relationships. Using a 28-day dyadic daily diary design of 142 parent-adolescent dyads, we examined how one’s own and one’s partner’s perceived response speed were associated with feelings of connection. Results revealed asymmetric and interdependent patterns. Faster response speed perceptions predicted greater connection, but these associations were more pronounced for parents. Additionally, parents’ perceptions of adolescents’ response speed predicted adolescents’ feelings of connection. These findings indicate that response speed perceptions can act as a mechanism that links connectivity to social connection in everyday life, but this depends on relational role.

articles.title: Two Decades of Change in Mexico–U.S. Migration, 2005–2025
articles.abstract: Mexican migration to the United States has undergone dramatic changes since reaching its peak two decades ago when it was considered the largest sustained population flow in the world. Previous research has documented a sharp decline in Mexico–U.S. migration in the late 2000s, but less is known about later trends. Studies also suggest that return migration to Mexico may have risen following an increase in removals from the United States. This study provides an update on the bidirectional flow of migrants between the two countries disaggregated by demographic subgroups using data from a quarterly employment survey in Mexico. Following the dramatic decline in the late 2000s, Mexican migration to the United States remained low for over a decade with only a modest increase in recent years. The rate of return migration to Mexico also declined sharply until the mid‐2010s and has remained low. Because return migration declined for longer than emigration, net emigration from Mexico has increased since 2010. The observed changes in Mexican migration in recent years are inconsistent with explanations that attribute the earlier decline to lower demand for immigrant labor in the United States and to the direct compositional effects of population aging in Mexico.

articles.title: To Work or Study? The Development of Adolescent Migration Expectations
articles.authors: Jennifer E. Glick, Melissa Alcaraz, Erick Axxe, Dirgha Ghimire
articles.abstract: Migration features regularly in young adult life course transitions in many low‐ and middle‐income countries. The aspirations–capabilities framework points to the importance of life goals and enabling resources for forming expectations of future moves. For some young people, moving away represents an opportunity to reach their aspirations. Others hold aspirations that are more easily fulfilled in the local setting. To understand how migration is connected to prior experiences and aspirations in adolescence, we focus on the formation of migration expectations, disaggregating expectations to include labor migration, education migration, and the expectation to avoid migration altogether. Relying on longitudinal data from adolescents in three diverse settings, Jalisco, Mexico ( n = 1593), Gaza Province, Mozambique ( n = 1350), and Chitwan, Nepal ( n = 1884), the analyses consider the mechanisms through which contemporary young cohorts form expectations for these different migration pathways. The results show that aspirations motivate distinct migration pathways with strikingly consistent patterns across settings. Educational aspirations are associated with subsequent expectations to migrate for further education, portending diversification of migration flows from low‐ and middle‐income settings where labor migration has predominated but access to formal education is expanding and youth engagement in education is growing.
